title: Clone, remotes and fetch
summary: A remote is another copy of the repository. Remote-tracking branches like origin/main are your last-known picture of it, and fetch updates that picture.

steps.title: Remotes
body: ```text
git clone https://github.com/acme/shop.git

Clone copies the **whole history** and sets up a **remote** named `origin` pointing at that URL. Nothing is linked live: from now on there are two independent repositories, and you exchange commits on purpose.
```text
git remote -v                       # list remotes and their URLs
git remote add upstream <url>       # add another (common with forks)
After cloning you have two kinds of branch:
```text
main            your local branch: you commit here
origin/main     remote-tracking branch: what main looked like on origin the last time you talked to it
You never commit to `origin/main`. It only moves when you `fetch`, `pull` or `push`.

steps.prompt: A teammate pushed two commits to `main` on GitHub ten minutes ago. You have not run any Git command since. Where does your `origin/main` point?
options: At the old commit: remote-tracking branches only update when you talk to the remote
At the new commit: Git syncs in the background
steps.explain: `origin/main` is a snapshot from your last fetch. That is why `git status` can say *up to date* while the server has moved on.

steps.title: fetch: download, change nothing else
body: `git fetch` downloads new commits from the remote and moves your **remote-tracking** branches. Your own branches and files are untouched.
```text
before fetch:   A---B   main, origin/main
after fetch:    A---B   main
C---D   origin/main
Now you can look before you integrate:
```text
git log --oneline main..origin/main   # what they did that I do not have
git diff main origin/main             # how the code differs
`git pull` is `git fetch` **plus** integrating `origin/main` into your branch (merge by default, or rebase). Fetch is always safe; pull changes your branch.

steps.prompt: You are on `main` at B. `origin/main` was at B too. A teammate pushed C and D. You run `git fetch`. What does `git log --oneline main..origin/main` print? (Messages are the letters; newest first.)
steps.explain: `main..origin/main` means *reachable from origin/main but not from main*: the two new commits. Your `main` has not moved yet.

steps.prompt: Which commands change your local branch `main`?
steps.explain: Fetch only updates `origin/*`. Merging or rebasing (which `pull` does for you) is what moves your branch.

steps.prompt: Match the name to what it is.
pairs: the default name of the remote you cloned from
your last-known copy of main on origin
a conventional name for the original repo when you work on a fork

steps.title: Ahead, behind, diverged
body: `git status` compares your branch with its **upstream** (usually `origin/main`) by counting commits:
```text
A---B---C   main               "Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit."
^origin/main                 -> push it
A---B   main                   "Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 2 commits,
\                            and can be fast-forwarded."  -> pull it
C---D origin/main
A---B---X   main               "Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged,
\                            and have 1 and 2 different commits each, respectively."
C---D origin/main          -> pull (merge or rebase), then push
Remember: these counts are only as fresh as your last fetch.

steps.prompt: Local `main` is `A---B---X---Y`. After `git fetch`, `origin/main` is `A---B---C`. What does the second line of `git status` print?
steps.answer: Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged, and have 2 and 1 different commits each, respectively.
steps.explain: X and Y are only local (2); C is only on origin (1). Git prints it over two lines; here it is one line.
accept:
Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged,
and have 2 and 1 different commits each, respectively.

steps.prompt: Complete the commands: download from every remote and delete remote-tracking branches that no longer exist on the server.
steps.explain: `--prune` removes stale `origin/feature-x` entries for branches someone deleted on the server. Many people set `git config --global fetch.prune true`.

steps.title: Fetch, compare, prune
prompt: `~/shop` is your clone of the team repo (its `origin` is `/srv/git/shop.git`, a bare repository standing in for GitHub). You have one commit that is not pushed. Since your last fetch, a teammate pushed to `main` and deleted the old branch `feature/old` on the server.
1. Download everything new **and** drop remote-tracking branches that no longer exist on the server. Do not change your local `main`.
2. Save how far `main` is ahead of and behind `origin/main` in `~/answers/ahead-behind.txt`, as two numbers: `ahead behind`.
3. Your local branch `feature/old` now tracks a branch that is gone. Delete it (its experiment was abandoned).

checks.name: origin/main is up to date
checks.fail: `origin/main` does not show the teammate's commits yet. `git fetch` downloads them.

checks.name: origin/feature/old is pruned
checks.fail: `origin/feature/old` is still there. `git fetch --prune` removes remote-tracking branches whose server branch was deleted.

checks.name: your local main did not move
checks.fail: Local `main` changed. Fetch only downloads; `pull` would also merge. Press Reset scenario.

checks.name: ahead-behind.txt says 1 ahead, 2 behind
checks.fail: `~/answers/ahead-behind.txt` should hold `1 2`. `git rev-list --left-right --count main...origin/main` prints ahead and behind.

checks.name: the stale local branch is deleted
checks.fail: Local `feature/old` still exists. `git branch -vv` marks it `gone`; delete it with `git branch -D` (it was never merged).

hints: `git fetch --prune` (or `git fetch -p`). Make it permanent with `git config --global fetch.prune true`.
`git status -sb` shows `[ahead 1, behind 2]`; `git rev-list --left-right --count main...origin/main` prints `1	2`.
`git branch -vv` lists `[origin/feature/old: gone]`. `git branch -D feature/old` deletes it.
steps.explain: Without `--prune`, remote-tracking branches pile up forever and `git branch -a` lies about what exists. `fetch.prune = true` is a common global setting. A branch whose upstream is `gone` was usually merged (often squash-merged) and deleted by the platform; check its log before `-D`.
